doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: What she teaches and why music is her calling
summary: She criticizes teachers who do not perform, describes her performance-based teaching, and says preserving the music is her calling.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: didn’t take her, because strangely enough the depth of her lyric singing, she doesn’t have any depth there, but when she improvised she never used shoobie-doobies. She had a wonderful way of singing over changes with a very, very light, lovely syllables and ideas. Little sweet ideas. So that surprised me. But I didn’t know that before, the thing. And after that I said, “Now you do that quite well,” I said, “but you need to go out there and listen to these monsters and know what’s going on.” But I think that maybe too, I have to say in support of the schools that they’re finding their way too. It’s new. So I think little by little, hopefully, they’re finding their way and they’ll have a different approach eventually, or maybe just not being so hard on these kids. I find a lot of the teachers that are teaching don’t play out. They don’t go out and do sessions. What do they know about it? What do they know about falling on their faces. You know, “Oh what do you play?” “Well I used to play—” whatever. You know? But they don’t go out and do it. So how can you teach the performance you see? What I teach is my own way, which is performance. A lot of it has to do with performance, getting it together, getting music together, getting lead sheets together, knowing how to count time, knowing what a chorus is, knowing how to get in and out and learning the melodies of the tunes, learning the roots, learning how to sing on changes, learning how to sing over the changes. You know? When they’re ready. But even in singing lyrics you know [clock] sings. See? But it stopped, it didn’t go twelve, didn’t go one.
We’re up to the half, the bridge.
Right. Pretty soon we’ll be on the out chorus.
If I see you go like this I know that we’ve got to go out.

No, if anybody goes out, you’re going out because I’ll sit here all day and talk about this because I love this music. Anything I can do to preserve it and keep it alive is what I’m here for. This is my calling, whether I’m talking to you and Tim, whether I’m teaching it, whether I’m singing it or whether I’m just listening to it. It’s my calling.
